2.text:
What is Warcrow?
Warcrow is a miniatures game set in the
fantastic world of Lindwurm, where players
control a small military force composed of
warriors, creatures, and spellcasters, engaging in
skirmishes to further their faction’s interests.
Before starting the game, players must select an
adventure to play. Each Warcrow adventure has
different conditions and requirements necessary
to achieve victory. Players then prepare the
game table and deploy the indicated terrain
elements, which can include fences, forests,
buildings, etc. Players then choose their faction
and create the army list that best suits their
strategy and plans for victory. The game begins
once both sides’ troops have been deployed.
Each adventure has a variable number of game
rounds, which continue until the end-of-game
conditions are met. In each round, players will
take turns activating their units. They can be
moved across the battlefield, attack opponents,
cast powerful spells, and more, until the
objectives of the adventure have been achieved.
The player who has accumulated the most
Victory Points (VP) wins the game.

5.text:
Basic Concepts
How to Resolve
Contradictions
In the event that two or more rules contradict
each other, follow the following conflict
resolution guide, ordered from highest to
lowest priority:
1.	If a rule states that an effect cannot be
applied (written in bold), then this prohibition
takes precedence over everything else.
2.	The adventure rules prevail over the unit
game profiles and the rules in this book.
3.	The unit’s game profiles take precedence
over the rules in this book.
4.	If the conflict occurs during a unit’s activation,
the player controlling that unit decides the
order in which the rules are resolved.
5.	In any other case, the player with the
initiative has the final say.
Miniatures: Troops and
Units
Every warrior and creature participating in the
battle is represented on the game table by a
miniature. In Corvus Belli’s Warcrow range,
players will find high-quality miniatures, sculpted
with great detail to showcase the dynamism
and tension of combat, the personality of the
leaders, and the equipment they carry.
5

6.text:
The rules contained in this book explain how to
move and fight with miniatures, as well as how
to interact with the terrain elements.
All miniatures must be mounted on the bases
included in the product box. These bases
represent the space occupied by the miniature,
although their size may vary. Under no
circumstances may the bases overlap during the
course of the game.
During a game of Warcrow, there will be
times when players will need to move their
opponent’s miniatures or game elements. In
these cases, remember to ask permission before
handling them or tell the opponent where they
should be placed. Assembling and painting the
miniatures is an equally important part of the
hobby, and the time and effort dedicated to it
should be respected.
The group of units under a player’s control is
their company, the military force that will face
off against their opponent’s to achieve victory
on the battlefield (See “Recruit a Company”).
From here on, all individual miniatures will
be referred to as troops. Thus, a mounted
Hegemony Hetman, an Orc Hunter, and a Rock
Troll are all considered troops.
Units are groupings of one or more troops,
and their game information is presented on a
profile card.
6

7.text:
Number of Troops Per Unit
Each Warcrow box contains exactly the
miniatures and profile cards needed to play
with the units purchased. In addition, each card
specifies the number of troops that make up
the unit.
Leader
Units must always have a designated troop
acting as the leader. The main function of the
troop leader is to serve as the reference point
for determining movement, as well as indicating
which troops are in formation and what actions
the unit is performing.
A unit that consists of a single troop, such as
Characters, are considered their own leader.
Following the Leader
All troops in the unit must follow the actions
of their leader at all times. If the leader charges
into combat, the other troops charge the same
target. If the leader does not engage the enemy
in combat, no other troop in the unit may do
so. If the leader cannot fire on a target because
it is out of range or lacks Line of Sight (LoS),
the unit will not fire, even if some of its troops
do have the target within range and LoS.
If the troop leader is taken out of combat,
a new troop leader must be designated
immediately.

12.text:
Games Profile Text
The rules and effects in the game profiles are
written in the second person (you), referring to
the unit that possesses them. For example, the
restriction “during your activation” refers to the
unit’s activation.
Personalities of Lindwurm
Some products in the Warcrow range include
a miniature that is designed to represent
both the standard version of the unit and a
named Lindwurm character. For example, the
same miniature can represent both a generic
unit such as the Hetman of the Hegemony of
Embersig, as well as a named character, such as
Drago the Anvil.
Allied, Enemy, and Neutral
Units
All units controlled by a player within their
company are allied with each other. All units
controlled by their opponent are considered
enemies.
In some adventures, neutral units may be
deployed or appear. These units have their
own profile but do not belong to either side.
The rules regarding their use are described
in their profile or in the adventure itself. (See
“Adventures”).
12

13.text:
Allied Unit Skills and “Other
Units”
Every unit is considered an ally of itself. When
the text of an effect, action, or passive skills of
a unit indicates that it affects “an allied unit,”
“allied units,” or “your allies,” it includes the
unit itself. However, if the text indicates that it
affects “other units” (allied or not), that primary
unit is excluded.
Units and Formation
All troops in a unit, whenever possible, must be
in formation. A troop is in formation with its
unit if:
•	 It is no more than 2 strides away from its
troop leader.
•	 Its troop leader has Line of Sight (LoS) to it
(see “Line of Sight”).
See “Appendix, Examples: 1. Units and
Formation” for more information.
Broken Formation
The moment at least one of the troops in a
unit is more than 2 strides away from the troop
leader, or the troop leader loses LoS to it, the
formation becomes broken.
When a unit with a broken formation is
activated, they can only perform the move
action. If the first move action is sufficient
to restore the formation, the player can
then declare any other action as usual (see
“Activating a Unit” and “Move”). Otherwise, the
second action must be used to move again.
13

14.text:
The troops of a unit cannot break formation
voluntarily. If it is impossible for a troop to
remain in formation, it must position itself as
close as possible to the troop leader.
Distances and
Measurements
Distances in Warcrow are expressed in strides.
One stride is equivalent to the radius of an
infantry base (15 mm).
Warcrow uses two templates to measure
distances: one short template and one long
template. All measurements between any two
game elements on the battlefield are taken from
base to base in the case of miniatures, or using
the edge of their base in the case of a terrain
element.
Distance between game elements can be
measured at any time and for any reason.
Line of Sight (LoS)
A unit’s Line of Sight (LoS) represents
everything it can see on the battlefield.
A unit has LoS to another unit if the troop
leader can draw a straight line between its base
and the base of at least half of the other unit’s
troops (rounded up). This line is not valid if it
passes through any game element that blocks
the LoS (such as miniatures from other units or
a building).
14

15.text:
While checking LoS, please note that:
•	 A troop always has LoS to itself and adjacent
troops.
•	 The troops that make up a unit do not block
LoS for their troop leader.
•	 All other units (allied, enemy, and neutral)
block the LoS.
•	 Miniatures have a 360º viewing angle, so LoS
can be traced from any point on their base.
•	 The lines that join the center of the base of
troops of the same unit (as long as they are in
formation) block LoS to other game elements.
•	 Terrain elements with the keyword “Blocks
LoS” prevent LoS from being drawn through
them (See “Terrain”).
•	 When checking LoS to a unit, the troops
that comprise it do not block LoS to other
members of the unit. For example, when
drawing LoS to a unit of Orc Hunters, those
in the front do not block those behind them.
•	 A unit has LoS to a terrain element if the
troop leader can draw a straight line from
any point on its base to any point on the base
of the terrain.
•	 Units engaged in combat can only draw LoS
to themselves, to adjacent units, or units they
are engaged with.
LoS can be checked at any time to prevent
actions from being declared against targets that
do not have LoS.
See “Appendix, Examples: 2. Line of Sight (LoS)”
for more information.
15

16.text:
Range
All ranged attacks, as well as some skills, specify
a range which the target must be within. When
checking the distance between a unit and
another game element, always measure the
distance from the troop leader.
If the target is another unit, measure the
shortest distance between the bases of the
leader and the closest troop in the target unit
(it doesn’t have to be their leader).
If the target is a terrain element measure the
shortest distance between the leader and the
base of the terrain.
See “Appendix, Examples: 3. Range” for more
information.
Target “within X strides”
When it is indicated that the target of an effect
must be “within X strides,” the distance must
be between 0 and X strides.
See “Appendix, Examples: 4. Target “within X
strides”.
Adjacent
A game element is adjacent to another if the
distance between them is 0.
A unit is adjacent to a terrain element if the
unit leader’s base is in contact with the terrain’s
base.
16

17.text:
Dice and Symbols
Warcrow uses a series of eight-sided dice,
differentiated by their color, which contain the
following symbols:
[success symbol]  - Success
[hollow success symbol]  - Hollow Success
[block symbol]  - Block
[hollow block symbol]  - Hollow Block
[special symbol]  - Special
[hollow special symbol]  - Hollow Special
These are the Warcrow dice and the symbols
that can be obtained on them:
17

18.text:
Offensive and Defensive Dice
The red  [red die] , orange  [orange die] , and yellow  [yellow die]  dice are
used for offense. These dice can yield the  [success symbol]
symbol, which represents a favorable outcome
in both attack and skill rolls.
The green  [green die] , blue  [blue die] , and black  [black die]  dice are
used for defense. These dice have the  [block symbol]  symbol,
which represents a favorable defense roll.
The  [special symbol]  symbols give troops the possibility to
activate special skils and other interactions (See
“Switches”).
The hollow versions  [hollow success symbol]   [hollow block symbol]   [hollow special symbol]  of the symbols are
only valid in certain situations, such as during
switches (See “Switches”).
Dice Rolls
Some unit attributes or values ​are represented
by a combination of dice that players will roll
with the icons representing the color-specific
dice. For example,  [orange die]  [orange die]
[orange die]  [orange die]  [blue die]  means a player must
roll 2 orange dice and 1 blue die.
Automatic symbols may appear next to
these icons, which must be added to the result
obtained. For example,  [orange die]  [success symbol]  means a player
must roll 1 orange die and add 1 [success symbol]  to the result.
Players cannot roll more than three dice of the
same color under any circumstances.
18

19.text:
Type of Dice Rolls
In Warcrow, there are two types of dice rolls,
depending on who is participating in them:
•	 Simple Roll: Only one player rolls the dice.
•	 Face to Face Roll: Both players roll the
dice at the same time, with the intention of
influencing the other’s outcome.
Simple Roll
In a Simple Roll, only one player participates by
following these steps:
1.	Create the dice pool. Gather the
dice indicated for the action about to be
performed. If any rule or effect allows dice to
be added or removed, apply it now. If the unit
includes a Character, also add their bonuses.
2.	Roll the dice. If any rule or effect allows the
dice to be repeated, apply it now.
3.	Add automatic symbols, if applicable.
These are added directly to the dice roll
result.
4.	Cancel dice and symbols. Apply these
effects now, if applicable.
5.	Apply switches. The player can spend as
many symbols as they want to apply any
number of switches that the roll has available
(see “Switches”).
6.	Determine the outcome. The result of the
roll consists of all the symbols that haven’t
been canceled or spent applying switches.
If at least 1 [success symbol]  symbol is obtained, the player
succeeds on the roll; otherwise, they fail.
19

20.text:
Occasionally, a roll will require 2 or more  [success symbol]
results to be considered successful. In these
cases, the required number of  [success symbol]  results is
indicated in parentheses; for example: “(2 [success symbol] )”.
Face to Face Roll
In a Face to Face Roll, both players participate
at the same time, so their rolls affect each other.
Follow these steps to resolve it:
1.	Create the dice pool. Take the dice
indicated for the action about to be
performed. If any rule or effect allows more
dice to be added or forces the player to
remove them, do so now. If the units include
a Character, add their bonuses as well.
2.	Roll the dice at the same time. If any rule or
effect allows the dice to be rerolled, apply it
now.
3.	Add automatic symbols to rolls, if
applicable.
4.	Cancel dice and symbols. Apply these
effects now, if applicable.
5.	Apply switches. The active player can spend
as many symbols as they want from their roll
to apply any number of switches available for
this turn. Then, their opponent will have the
same opportunity to apply their switches
(see “Switches”).
6.	Block successes. Each  [block symbol]  cancels 1 [success symbol]  from
the opponent.
7.	Determine the outcome. The symbols
that have not been canceled out are the
result of both rolls. Each player resolves the
effects of the symbols they still have in their
20

21.text:
roll. If at least 1 [success symbol]  is obtained, the player
succeeds on the roll; otherwise, they fail.
Sometimes players will have to resolve Face to
Face Rolls “against the system.” An example of
this would be combat against a neutral, Hostile
unit. In this case, the opponent will make all
the decisions on behalf of the system, such as
applying switches.
See “Appendix, Examples: 5. Face to Face Roll”
for more information.
Switches
Switches allow players to spend some of
the symbols obtained from rolling the dice to
activate special effects before determining
the outcome.
Available switches can be found in a unit’s
profile:
2
1
2
1.	Requirement: The symbols that must be
spent to activate the switch.
2.	Effect: The rules that apply when the switch
is activated.
Please note that:
•	 Each symbol spent on a switch can no longer
be used in other switches, effects, or to
determine the result of a roll.
21

22.text:
•	 The same switch can be activated multiple
times, as long as the player has enough
symbols to do so.
•	 You may activate a switch even if its effects
cannot be applied, or can only be applied
partially. For example, a symbol can be spent
on a switch that heals 1 [damage] , even if a unit hasn’t
suffered any damage.
•	 A switch can only be used in the roll to
which it is associated.
If a switch has multiple effects, these are
applied in the order in which they are written.
For example:
“Cancel 1 [block symbol]  from your target and
add 1 [success symbol]  to your roll.”
Even if the opponent didn’t obtain any  [block symbol]  to
cancel, the player can still add the  [success symbol]  to their
roll.
Switches and Tinge
Some switches may require spending 1 or more
[Tinge]  tokens to activate. The indicated  [Tinge]  tokens
must be spent as a requirement to activate the
switch and apply its effects.
22

23.text:
Preparing the Game
Before the game can begin, the following
preparations must be followed in the order
shown:
1.	Prepare the game table.
2.	Choose an adventure.
3.	Recruit a company.
4.	Form Command Token Reserve (COM).
5.	Decide who has initiative.
6.	Prepare terrain elements
7.	Choose the deployment zone.
8.	Deploy units.
Once these steps have been completed, players
can begin the first round (See “Playing the
Game”)!
1. Prepare the Game Table
The first thing needed to play a game of
Warcrow is a firm surface on which to place all
the game elements, referred to as the game
table. The battlefield, in which the game will
take place, must be clearly defined on the game
table. The standard size for an adventure is
90 cm x 90 cm.
It is recommended to ensure there is enough
space on the table to accommodate the
battlefield, all the game elements (the turn
counter, profile cards, dice, tokens, etc.), and the
rulebook.
23

24.text:
2. Choose an Adventure
Both opponents must agree on an adventure
among the free downloadable adventures on
the official Warcrow website: https://warcrow.
com/resources/warcrow
All adventures contain the necessary
information to set up the deployment zones for
the units, the specific use of terrain elements,
and, most importantly, the victory and end-of-
game conditions. All of this detailed information
can be found in the “Adventures” chapter of
this rulebook.
It is essential that both players fully understand
the rules and victory conditions of the
adventure. If necessary, clarify with each other
any doubts that may arise after reading the
specifications of the adventure that is going to
be played.
3. Recruit a Company
Now understanding the specifics of the
adventure, it’s time for players to recruit the
units that will make up their company. Always
keep in mind the features of the adventure and
the strategy planned to use to achieve victory.
24

25.text:
Agree on the Size
of the Game
Players must agree on the number of army
points available to recruit companies. In a
standard Warcrow game, this will be 250
points. Experienced players can vary that
number for more of a challenge.
All the adventures are designed to be played
with 250 points, but if a different point total
is agreed on for the game, it is recommended
to adjust the number of turns per round
accordingly.
Choose a Faction
Each faction has its own play style and offers
different tools to achieve victory in each
adventure. Players should choose the one that
best suits their playstyle or whose aesthetic
appeals to them the most – assembling and
painting miniatures is an essential part of this
hobby, so players choose the faction that they
find most visually appealing.
Select a Commander
From among all the Officer Characters in
a faction, choose one and name them
the commander of the company. (See
“Characters”). Some Characters have the High
Command characteristic, which means that
if included in a company, they automatically
become the commander.
25

26.text:
More than one High Command character
cannot be included in a company.
Deduct the cost of the commander from the
total army points available to recruit a company.
Decide the Rest of the Units
Once a commander has been selected, as many
units as players want can be added by paying
their cost in army points, provided the following
requirements are met:
•	 The sum of the costs of all the units in the
company must be equal to or less than the
total army points agreed upon for the game
(250 points for the standard game).
•	 Players cannot include more copies of
the same unit in their company than its
availability value (AVB).
It’s not necessary to spend exactly the total
army points. For example, for a 250-point game,
players can create a company with a total cost
of 240 points.
4. Form Command Token
Reserve (COM)
Players add up the total COM (Command)
value of all the units recruited for their
company and take as many command tokens as
the total obtained. That becomes the command
pool.
26

27.text:
Command tokens represent the leadership
capacity of some units in the company, allowing
units to activate command skills, powerful
effects that can sometimes tip the balance of
the battle (see “Skills”).
Spent command tokens are not recovered
(unless the effects of one of a unit or the
adventure allow it).
5. Decide Who Has
Initiative
To determine who will have the initiative,
players will have to resolve a Face to Face Roll:
•	 Gather  [orange die]  [yellow die]  dice.
•	 The person with the most COM adds  [orange die]  to
their roll.
•	 The player who rolls the most  [success symbol]  decides
whether to keep the Initiative Token or give it
to their opponent. In case of a tie, repeat the
roll until one player rolls more  [success symbol] .
Whoever has the initiative decides:
•	 Who starts by deploying their units (see step
8).
•	 Who will be the first to activate in the first
round.
Whoever does not have the initiative:
•	 Decides who starts by placing the first
terrain element (see step 6).
•	 Chooses a deployment zone (see step 7).
27

28.text:
6. Prepare Terrain
Elements
The player who does not have the initiative
decides who will start by placing the first
terrain element anywhere on the battlefield.
Both players must each place at least one, then
they will take turns placing terrain elements
until a satisfactory amount has been placed or
all available terrain has been used.
Number of Terrain Elements
We cannot provide strict rules on the
characteristics of placed terrain or how many
pieces to deploy on the battlefield, because we
do not want to limit player imagination when
creating their own or using pieces already
owned. Below are some tips that can serve as a
guide for players’ first games:
•	 Place at least two terrain elements where the
base has a surface area equivalent to a square
with sides measuring between 7 and 10
strides, and which would affect movement or
LoS. For example: forests, hills, a lake, or ruins.
•	 Place up to two buildings or up to four small
structures.
•	 Place up to four fences, barricades, or walls.
In the “Terrain” chapter, more information is
provided on how to define terrain and the
recommended dimensions.
Distance Between Terrain
28

29.text:
Elements
Arrange the terrain so that the resulting
adventure is playable for both companies.
Creating dead ends or overlapping elements can
negatively impact gaming experience, so terrain
should be spaced at least 2 strides apart, with
the exception of fences or barricades. However,
this could be a challenge that experienced
players agree to beforehand.
Placing terrain elements within 5 strides of an
adventure objective is also not recommended,
as these are points where most of the units will
converge (See “Adventures”).
7. Choose the Deployment
Zone
The player who does not have the initiative
chooses the deployment zone they will use
to place their units on the battlefield. Their
opponent will use the remaining zone to deploy.
8. Deploy Units
The player who has the initiative decides
which side deploys one of its units first. Each
player takes turns deploying one unit at a time
until all units have been deployed.
To deploy a unit, place all of its miniatures
within the boundaries of the deployment zone
– all of their bases must be entirely within the
player’s deployment zone and the boundaries of
the battlefield. All troops in the unit must be in
formation (See “Units and Formation”).
29

30.text:
It is crucial that both players thoroughly
understand the rules for their units. If necessary,
clarify any questions about the rules beforehand
to avoid arguments that could disrupt the
friendly atmosphere and flow of the game.
Playing the Game
30

31.text:
The battlefield is set, the objectives are clear,
and players have recruited their company that
they hope will secure the victory. It’s time to
roll the dice!
A game of Warcrow unfolds over a series of
game rounds (or simply, rounds), divided into
turns in which players alternate activating their
units.
The game ends when either player meets the
victory conditions or they have played the
maximum number of rounds indicated by the
adventure.
Turn Counter
The turn counter has ten
numbered positions, each
corresponding to a game
turn. The central dial has
an arrow that points to
the current game turn.
A number of game
elements are tracked here – when potential
adventure events occur, how long spell effects
last, and when demoralized units can rally. All
of these are represented by tokens placed on
the turn counter when the rules indicate. When
placing a token on a position that already has
another token, place it on top to form a stack.
“End of Round” Token
31

32.text:
This token indicates which turn will end the
current round, after unit activations and the
resolution of events or effects. This token must
always be at the bottom of a formed stack.
Game Rounds
Each round consists of the following phases:
•	 Start of the round
•	 Turn phase
•	 End of the round
Again, please take note: “round” and “turn” are
two different concepts. A round is composed of
several turns.
Start of the Round
At the beginning of the first round, set the turn
counter dial to position “1” and place the “End of
Round” token on the position indicated by the
adventure rules. For example, if the adventure
states that each round consists of four turns,
place the “End of Round” token on position “4.”
Next, all effects that indicate they apply “at
the start of the round” take place. Each effect
must be applied and resolved in order, one after
another. First, the adventure effects are applied,
and then the effects of both companies are
resolved. If both players have effects to apply,
the player with the initiative decides which side
executes all of its effects first, as well as the
order in which the effects are applied.
Turn Phase
32

33.text:
Each round consists of a number of turns in
which players alternate activating their units. If
it’s the first turn of the round, the player with the
initiative decides who activates a unit first and
who goes second. This activation order remains
the same until the end of the round. The
number of turns is indicated by the position of
the “End of Round” token on the turn counter.
When the turn has resolved where this token is
located, the round ends.
Each turn of the game has the following order:
1.	Company A activates one of their units.
2.	Company B activates one of their units.
3.	Events.
Once both players have finished all activations,
check the turn counter for any unresolved
events and advance the dial one position. If one
of the effects indicated by the dial is the “End
of Round” token, the current round ends (See
“End of Round”). Otherwise, proceed to play
out another game turn.
Start and End of Turn
When an effect needs to be resolved with
the conditions of “at the start of a turn,”
apply it before any activations. Effects with the
conditions of “at the end of the turn” should
be applied after both players’ activations, but
before the event phase.
Pass
33

34.text:
If a player has already activated all of their units
on the battlefield (excluding demoralized units),
they may choose to pass without activating a
unit. If the opponent also passes, advance the
dial on the turn counter to the “End of Round”
token (triggering all effects along the way). Treat
this turn as the last one of the current round.
If the opponent does not pass, the passing
player will have another opportunity to activate
a unit or pass on the next turn.
If no units can be activated, the player must
pass.
Events
Check if any events are triggered on the turn
counter, as well as manage active effects or
demoralized units.
To complete this phase, perform the following
steps:
1.	Resolve the effects indicated by the tokens in
the current position the turn dial is pointed
to, one by one, starting with the top token.
After resolving each token, remove it (except
for the “End of Round” token).
2.	If the “End of Round” token is in the current
turn position, always resolve it last. Apply all
the steps of the “End of Round” phase to
resolve it. If the requirements for ending the
game are not met, start a new round.
3.	The marker advances one position. If it’s in
34

35.text:
position 10, that means it moves to position 1.
Event Tokens
The adventure rules may indicate that events
will be triggered at the end of certain turns.
These are represented by “Event Tokens.” These
tokens are placed on the turn counter at the
position indicated by the adventure, and when
they are triggered, the associated event takes
effect (see “Adventures”).
For example, the adventure indicates that the “Rain” event
is triggered on the sixth turn, so an event token is placed
on position “6” of the turn counter. When turn six ends, the
event token is removed and the effects indicated in the
adventure under the heading “Rain” are applied.
Demoralized Unit Tokens
When placed on the turn counter, each of these
tokens represents a unit that is demoralized.
When this token is resolved, the associated
unit will attempt to rally, or otherwise it must
flee again (See “Stress and Morale, Demoralized
Unit”).
End of the Round
35

36.text:
All effects that apply “at the end of the round”
take place, and each one must be applied
and resolved in order, one after another. The
adventure effects must be applied first, and then
the effects of both companies are resolved. If
both players have effects to apply, the player
with the initiative decides which side executes
all of its effects first. Each player decides the
order in which their effects are applied.
Once all effects that occur “at the end of
the round” have been resolved, perform the
following steps in order:
Victory Points
Victory Points (VP) are earned by controlling
objectives or fulfilling the adventure’s
requirements. Players calculate their total VP
now and check if they have achieved victory to
end the game (See “Adventures”).
Reduce Stress
Reduce the stress on the units that are not
demoralized. (See “Stress and Morale”).
•	 Reduce the stress level by a maximum of
two levels for units that were not activated
during the round. These units do not have an
activation token.
•	 Then, reduce the stress level by 1 for the
units that were activated (those with an
activation token).
Check for Effects of the Tinge
36

37.text:
Units that have at least 1 [Tinge]  in their profile must
deal with the effects of the Tinge (see “Magic,
Effects of the Tinge”).
No One Gets Left Behind
Whoever has the initiative decides who
performs this step first. All units on the
battlefield that do not have an activation token
on their profile can perform the move action
once (see “Activating a Unit, Move”) or the
[long action] Rest action (see “Activating a Unit, Rest”) if
they meet these requirements:
•	 They are not demoralized.
•	 They are not engaged in combat.
Remove Activation Tokens
Players remove activation tokens from all units.
Change of Initiative
Whichever player has fewer Victory Points (VP)
will have the initiative during the next round. In
case of a tie, the initiative token changes hands
to whoever did not have initiative last round.
Advance the “End of Round”
Token
If the requirements to end the game are not
met, a new round begins. Move the token
forward as many spaces as there are turns per
round indicated in the adventure, and continue
the game.
End of the Game
37

38.text:
When players meet the requirements that end
the adventure, or when the maximum number
of rounds have been played, the game ends. The
player that has accumulated the most VP will be
the winner. In case of a tie, the adventure will
indicate how to resolve it, if possible.
Activating a Unit
When a player declares that one of their units is
activating, they place an activation token on its game
profile. If it already has one assigned, the unit will
suffer 1 stress instead. (See “Stress and Morale”).
During its activation, a unit can perform:
A.	Up to two simple actions. Any combination
of them. The only action that can be repeated
is moving.
» Move
» Attack
» Perform a combat skill
» Perform a Tinge skill
» Perform a magic skill
B.	A single  [long action] long action:
»  [long action] Assault
»  [long action] Charge
»  [long action] Rest
Units may have skills (combat, Tinge, or magic)
with the  [long action]  icon at the beginning of their name.
In these cases, performing the skill requires
a long action instead of a simple action, thus
exhausting the unit’s entire activation.
Declare an Action
38

39.text:
The first step in performing an action is
declaring it. The requirements for an action
must be met before it can be declared. Any
effects related to the declaration of an action
must be resolved before any of the action’s
effects are applied. For example, the  [long action]  Assault
action is composed of two simple actions: move
and attack. Each of these is declared before
being performed.
If the effects of a single action include
performing—and therefore declaring—another
action, this second action does not count
toward the action limit of the activation.
See “Appendix, Examples: 6. Activating a Unit
and Declaring an Action”.
At the End of the Activation
At the end of a unit’s activation, players must
follow these steps:
1.	 Effects and skills. Apply game effects
and skills that trigger “at the end of the
activation”.
2.	 Stress. All units whose stress level exceeds
their MOR value must make a successful
WP roll to avoid becoming demoralized and
fleeing (see “Stress and Morale”).
3.	 Contest for control of objectives. The
unit contests control of objectives within 3
strides (see “Adventures, Objectives”).
Some “at the end of the activation” skills allow
39

40.text:
other units to activate. Only one of those skills
may be used per activation (having priority the
player currently activating a unit). It’s effects
will be applied after contesting the control of
objectives.
Move
To perform this action, players must consult
the two “A-B” values ​of the unit’s movement
(MOV) attribute. Each of these two numbers
represents a distance, measured in strides,
that the unit can travel in any order the player
chooses. For example, if a unit has MOV 3-2, it
can move 3 strides and then 2 strides, or vice
versa: 2 strides and then 3 strides.
It is not mandatory for a unit to travel the
entire distance of each segment. In the above
example, MOV 3-2, players can move up to 3
strides and then up to 2 strides (and vice versa).
Any distance not covered during the first
segment is not carried over to the next.
Movement 0
A unit with a MOV value of 0 cannot use that
value to move across the battlefield.
For example, a unit with a MOV value of 3-0
that declares the move action can only perform
a single 3-stride movement.
40

41.text:
Templates
To move a unit, players place the short template
touching the edge of the base, making sure
they are using the side that corresponds to the
troop’s movement. The unit can move anywhere
from zero strides up to the end of the selected
distance.
The unit must be able to travel its path in a
straight line without obstacles. That is, its base
must be able to move without colliding with
the base of an enemy unit, a neutral unit, or
the base of a terrain element that prevents
movement (Impassable).
To perform movements of more than 5 strides,
players must use the long template. Just like
with the short template, the base must touch
the edge of the template, and then the unit may
move up to their allowed distance.
Notice that movement is measured from the
“front” to the “back” of the base. Therefore, the
indicated amount of movement is not the total
distance a unit travels, as this distance is the
one between the initial and final positions. To
calculate the total distance, the diameter of the
base itself needs to be factored in (marked on
the long template).
See “Appendix, Examples: 7A. Using Templates
For Movement”.
41

42.text:
Units Composed of Several
Troops
To move a unit composed of two or more
troops, follow these steps:
•	 Move the troop leader.
•	 Position the other troops in the unit in
formation (a maximum of 2 strides away from
the troop leader and with a LoS to them).
The troop leader ignores the other troops in
their unit during movement. If they end their
movement on top of one of the other troops
in their unit, remove that troop first, resolve
the troop leader’s movement, and then place
the removed troop back in formation with the
others.
See “Appendix, Examples: 7B. Moving Units
Composed of Several Troops”).
Keep in mind that:
•	 A unit can perform the move action but not
advance (travel distance 0).
•	 A unit can move through any terrain element
that does not have the Impassable keyword.
Other keywords may reduce a unit’s
movement capabilities (See “Terrain Element
Keywords”).
•	 A unit cannot end its movement on terrain
elements with the keyword Impassable or
Unstable. (See “Terrain Element Keywords”).
•	 A unit cannot end its movement in contact
with other enemy or neutral units.
42

43.text:
•	 A unit cannot move through the lines that
join the center of the bases of troops that
form another enemy or neutral unit (as long
as their members are in formation).
See “Appendix, Examples: 7C. Moving Through
Other Units”.
Engage in Combat
A unit is engaged in combat (or simply
engaged) with an enemy unit whenever at
least one of its troops is in base-to-base contact
with one or more troops of the enemy unit.
A unit engaged in combat:
•	 Cannot perform long actions.
•	 Cannot draw LoS to units that are not
adjacent or engaged with it.
Opportunity Attack
If a player declares a move action with a unit
that is engaged in combat, the enemy unit
engaged will have the opportunity to suffer
1 stress in order to perform an attack of
opportunity before the unit moves.
Steps to resolve an opportunity attack:
1.	 Declaration
The unit declaring the opportunity attack is
considered the attacker, and the enemy unit is
considered the defender.
43

44.text:
2.	 Face to Face Roll
A Face to Face Roll is performed between the
attacking unit’s attack roll and the defending
unit’s defense roll. During this roll, players
cannot apply switches or activate any
available modifiers.
3.	 Resolving the Attack
Each unit inflicts 1 [damage]  on its opponent for each
[success symbol]  it achieves in the dice roll result.
Once the Face to Face Roll has been resolved,
the unit will perform its movement. The enemy
unit cannot make an attack of opportunity if it
is demoralized.
See “Appendix, Examples: 8. Opportunity
Attack”.
44

45.text:
Attack
Most units have at least one attack listed in
their combat panel:
4
2
1
3
3
5
1.	Type. The attacks can be of two types:
ranged attacks (projectile attacks) or
melee attacks.
2.	Range. Distance within which the target of
the ranged attack must be.
3.	Attack roll. These are the dice players must
roll when performing an attack (they may be
accompanied by automatic symbols).
4.	Modifier. A unit can suffer 1 stress to add
the modifier value to the roll the player
makes (See “Face to Face Roll, Create the
dice pool”). Keep in mind that the unit must
be able to suffer stress, meaning it must have
less stress than its MOR value (See “Stress
and Morale”).
5.	Switches. Offer the possibility of spending
some of the symbols obtained in the attack
roll to apply various effects.
Modifiers and Tinge
Some modifiers show the  [Tinge]
symbol, indicating that the
unit will receive  [Tinge]  when
they are added.
45

46.text:
Melee Attack
A unit that is engaged in combat can initiate a
combat. The unit performing the action will
be the attacker, and its target will be the
defender.
Follow these steps to resolve a combat:
1.	Declaration
The attacking unit selects an enemy unit it
is already engaged with as the target of the
attack.
2.	Positioning Maneuvers
If any troops in the attacking unit are not
engaged in combat, they must perform
positioning maneuvers to join the fight (See
“Positioning Maneuvers”).
3.	Face to Face Roll
A Face to Face Roll is performed between
the attacking unit’s attack and the defending
unit’s defense. When creating the dice pool,
starting with the defending unit, units can
suffer 1 stress to add the associated modifier
to their roll.
4.	Attack Resolution
Each unit inflicts 1 [damage]  on its opponent for each
[success symbol]  it achieves in the dice roll result.
5.	Combat Result
The unit that inflicts the most  [damage]  on its
opponent is the winner of the combat, the
other is considered a defeated unit and
suffers 1 stress. If both units inflict the same
amount of damage, the combat ends in a
draw (neither unit is the winner nor the
defeated)
46

47.text:
When determining the damage ( [damage] ) caused by
each unit, add up all the damage inflicted from
the declaration of the attack until its resolution,
including that inflicted by skills or switches.
6.	Pushing Back the Defeated Unit
If both units are still engaged, the unit that
has won the combat has the option of
pushing back the defeated unit. Apply the
following steps:
1.	The defeated unit may suffer 1 stress to
avoid being pushed back. If it does, ignore
the remaining steps.
2.	The winning unit shoves the defeated unit
back a distance equal to the latter’s initial
MOV value. If the defeated unit has more
than one troop, when repositioning to
maintain formation, these troops should,
if possible, end up further away from the
victorious unit than their troop leader.
3.	If the winning unit is no longer engaged
in combat, it can choose to pursue the
defeated unit, moving entirely its first
movement value to end up as close as
possible to it.
If their troop leader touches the base of
a troop from the defeated unit, they will
remain engaged in combat.
See “Appendix, Examples: 9A. Melee Attacks,
Pushing Back the Defeated Unit”.
47

48.text:
4.	End of the Attack
If the victorious unit remains engaged, it must
perform positioning maneuvers. (See
“Positioning Maneuvers”).
If the winning unit is not engaged in combat
and the defeated unit was destroyed during
the attack, the winning unit can perform the
move action for free (it does not count as an
activation).
See “Appendix, Examples: 9B. Example of Melee
Attacks”.
Positioning Maneuvers
All troops in a unit are required to assist their
comrades when their unit attacks a target.
These maneuvers represent the attacking unit’s
attempts to gain ground against the defending
unit. To perform positioning maneuvers, a unit
must be engaged in combat. Follow these steps:
1.	If the troop leader is not engaged, swap it
with another troop in the unit that is engaged
with the target unit.
2.	There may be troops remaining in that unit
that are not engaged. Place them so that they
are.
When placing the troops of the unit performing
positioning maneuvers, the following rules must
be observed:
•	 Units cannot use positioning maneuvers to
engage in combat with units they have not
already engaged with.
•	 If it is impossible for a troop to engage
in combat (because there is no space or
48

49.text:
because doing so would break formation),
they must be placed in contact with their
troop leader – or, failing that, with any other
troop in their unit – as close as possible to
any enemy troop in the defending unit.
•	 If none of the above points are possible,
position the troops as close as possible to
their troop leader.
Multiple Combats
If a unit is engaged with more than one enemy
unit, its performance will be penalized. When
the player creates the attack or defense dice
pool, they must remove one die or automatic
symbol. This penalty also applies to opportunity
attack rolls.
Ranged Attacks
A unit that is not engaged in combat can
perform a ranged attack (if it has one). The unit
performing the action will be the attacker, and
its target will be the defender.
Follow these steps to resolve ranged attacks:
1.	Declaration
The attacking unit selects an enemy unit as
its target that it has LoS to and that is within
attack range.
2.	Face to Face Roll
A Face to Face Roll is performed between
the attacking unit’s ranged attack and the
defending unit’s defense.
When creating the dice pool, starting with the
defending unit. Units can suffer 1 stress to add
the associated modifier to their roll.
49

50.text:
In this roll, the defending unit:
» Can only use the defensive dice (green,
blue, and black) and the automatic symbols
[block symbol]  and  [hollow block symbol] ; all other dice and automatic
symbols are ignored.
» Cannot activate any switches.
3.	End of the Attack
The attacking unit inflicts 1 [damage]  on the
defending unit for each  [success symbol]  it achieves in the
dice roll result.
Units engaged in combat cannot resolve
ranged attacks.
See “Appendix, Examples: 10. Example of
Ranged Attacks”.
Cover
When a unit is targeted by a ranged attack,
it can benefit from cover if it is adjacent
to a game element (another unit or a
terrain element) with the Cover (D) keyword.
Additionally, another condition must be met
depending on whether or not the game element
blocks LoS:
•	 Blocks LoS (for example, by a miniature or
a building). The unit is in cover if the element
blocks the LoS to at least half of the troops
in the unit (rounding up).
•	 Does not block LoS (for example, by a
fence or a barricade). The unit is in cover
if, when drawing LoS to at least half of the
troops (rounding up), it has to pass through
the element.
50

51.text:
If a unit can benefit from several coverage
values, the player must choose one.
See “Appendix, Examples: 11. Cover”
Ranged Attack Into Combat
A unit can make a ranged attack against an
enemy unit that is engaged in combat. In this
case, the player must treat other units engaged
with their target as providing Cover ( [black die] ),
following the LoS and Cover rules. When an
attack is declared, the units engaged with the
target suffer 1 stress.
Perform a
Combat Skill
To perform this action, a unit must have at least
1 combat skill in its profile. Choose one of the
combat skills, verify that the requirements are
met, and apply its effects (See “Skills”).
Perform a Tinge Skill
To perform this action, a unit must have
at least 1 Tinge skill and 1 [Tinge]  in its profile.
Choose one of the Tinge skills, verify that the
requirements are met, spend 1 [Tinge] , and apply
the effects (See “Skills”).
51

52.text:
Perform a Magic Skill
Spellcasters can cast spells using their magic
skills. To perform this action, a unit must follow
the spellcasting steps (See “Magic”).
[long action] Assault
This action allows a unit to move to engage an
enemy unit and attack. When a player declares
this action, they must select a target enemy unit
(LoS is not required). This long action consists
of two simple actions that must be performed
in this order:
1.	Move. The troop leader of the unit must be
able to move, using both of the unit’s MOV
values, until it engages in combat with the
target unit – otherwise, this action cannot
be performed. Move the troop leader and
position the other troops in its unit in
formation. At this point, the unit is considered
to have assaulted. This step is an exception
to the rule that a unit performing a “Move”
cannot engage another unit. (See “Move”).
2.	Attack the target unit in melee. The unit
initiates combat with the enemy unit, which is
resolved by applying all the rules described in
“Melee Attack”.
52

53.text:
[long action] Charge
This action allows a unit to move in a straight
line to engage an enemy unit and attack. When
a player declares this action, they must select
a target enemy unit that they have LoS to. This
long action consists of two simple actions that
must be performed in this order:
1.	 Move. The troop leader must be able
to move in a straight line, using the unit’s
charging movement, until engaged with the
target unit – otherwise, this action cannot
be performed. Move the troop leader and
position the other troops of the unit in
formation. At this point, the unit is considered
to have charged. This step is an exception
to the rule that a unit performing a “Move”
cannot engage another unit.
2.	 Attack the target unit in melee. The unit
initiates combat with the enemy unit, which is
resolved by applying all the rules described in
“Melee Attack”.
Because the unit charged, it can repeat its
attack roll.
Hold and Shoot
When a player declares a charge or assault
against a unit with a ranged attack, the opposing
player may choose for the unit to suffer 1 stress
so that it may hold and shoot – if the unit has
LoS.
53

54.text:
•	 When a unit holds and shoots: resolve a
ranged attack against the enemy unit before
it moves, ignoring the ranged attack’s range.
During this attack, the firing unit cannot
activate any switches. Once the ranged attack
is resolved, the enemy unit proceeds with its
declared action.
[long action] Rest
When a unit performs this action, the player
may apply each of these options once:
•	 Eliminate all the unit’s stress.
•	 Remove a state of choice from the unit’s
profile.
•	 Remove 1 [Tinge]  from the unit’s profile.
•	 Perform a movement using only its first MOV
value.
54

55.text:
Skills
Skills are the set of effects and abilities that
units have in Warcrow. Skills are presented as
such:
2
1
3
4
1.	Type of skill
2.	Name of skill
3.	Requirements
4.	Effects
[long action] Long Action
Combat, Tinge, or Magic skills may include the
[long action]  icon at the beginning of their name. This
icon indicates that the skill requires the use of
a long action, instead of a simple action, to be
performed.
Requirements
To perform a skill, all the stated requirements
must be met. The following are different kind of
requirements:
•	 Line of Sight (LoS). All skills require LoS
to the target, unless the requirements specify
that they are No LoS.
•	 Limitation. Some skills have limitations on
their use. For example:
» Once per round
55

56.text:
Skills can only be performed once during the
specified timing in their requirements.
•	 Target. Determines the target (which can be
one or more) of the skill, as well as the range
within which they must be located to be
valid targets. A unit can target units that are
engaged in combat with its skills, following
the LoS rules.
Some skills in Warcrow affect more units than
just the target specified in the requirements.
When this happens, the unit performing the skill
only needs LoS to the target specified in the
requirements.
•	 Timing. This specifies the exact moment
when a player can perform the skill. Some
examples of timing include:
» At the beginning of your activation
» When you are the target of an attack
Some skills indicate that they are performed
during unit activation, whether allied or enemy
(such as: “during your activation”, “during the
target’s activation”, ...). These skills can be used
before or after an action (performed during
the activation), but not while the action is being
resolved.
•	 Duration. Some skill effects last over time.
These skills include the requirement: Duration:
X turns. When performing such skills, place
an effect token X positions ahead of the
current turn on the turn counter. The skill’s
effects will be active until the effect token
56

57.text:
is resolved, during the event phase of the
corresponding turn.
»  The effect tokens are numbered on one
side to make it easier to associate them
with the skills that share the same number.
» If a unit or terrain element is targeted by
a skill with a duration effect that is already
active, remove the previous effect tokens
and place the new ones without applying
any effect that happens when the duration
ends.
•	 Availability. Skills are only available while
the unit is on the battlefield and is not
demoralized, except if they have:
» Permanent. Skills with Permanent apply their
effects even if the unit is not present on
the battlefield, is destroyed, is demoralized,
or, in the case of a Character, joins another
unit (even if that skill is not present in its
character in a unit game profile).
» Dauntless. Skills with Dauntless apply their
effects even if the unit is demoralized.
Example of Permanent skill.
57

58.text:
Types of Skills
In Warcrow, there are several different types of
skills:
Combat Skills
These skills may be performed with the action
Perform a combat skill.
Magic Skills
Also known as “spells” (see “Magic”), Spellcasters
may perform these skills with the action
Perform a magic skill.
Tinge Skills
These skills require spending 1 [Tinge]  to perform.
They may be performed with the action
Perform a tinge skill.
58

59.text:
Command Skills
These skills require spending one command
token to use. Unlike the previous skills,
command skills do not require spending an
action. Furthermore, they are not limited to a
unit’s activation, but can be used whenever the
requirements are met.
Passive Skills
Passive skills have no cost for the unit and, as it
happens with command skills, they may be used
outside the unit’s activation as long as their
requirements are met.
59

60.text:
Magic
Spellcasters can make use of the magical skills
they have listed in their game profile.
Special Characteristics
of Magic Skills
Alterations
Magical skills can have alterations that allow
players to modify the characteristics of the spell.
More than one alteration can be applied during
the casting of a spell.
There are two types of alterations:
•	   [black die] : They allow the spell to be enhanced in
exchange for forcing the Spellcaster to make a
Tinge roll if the casting roll is successful.
•	   [Tinge] : Called “Tinge alterations,” these allow
the Spellcaster to spend  [Tinge]  tokens they have
on their game profile to enhance the spell.
They must have the necessary  [Tinge]  tokens
to declare their use during the first step of
casting.
Automatic
Magical skills may have the Automatic
requirement. In these cases, the spellcasting
steps will not be resolved; instead, their effects
will be applied directly, as if they were a combat
skill.
60

61.text:
Casting a Spell
Follow these steps to cast a spell:
1. Declaration
The player indicates which spell their unit
will cast and, if they wish to use them, the
alterations it will apply. They then select a game
element as their target that meets the spell’s
requirements.
2. Blocking the Spell
If the opponent wants to attempt to block the
spell, they must declare it now (see “Blocking a
Spell”).
3. WP Roll
Roll the Spellcaster’s WP.
Once, during the apply switches step, the
Spellcaster can receive 1 [Tinge]  in order to add 1 [success symbol]
to their roll.
If the roll is a success, the Spellcaster has cast
their spell and must spend as much  [Tinge]  as
indicated by the applied Tinge alterations.
4. Apply the Effects of the Spell
If the spell succeeds in being cast, apply the
effects of the spell, taking into consideration the
altered properties.
61

62.text:
5. Applying the Consequences of the
Tinge
1.	If a player has successfully cast the spell and
applied  [black die]  alterations, they must perform a
Tinge roll (see “Tinge Roll”).
2.	If the Spellcaster received  [Tinge]  on the WP
roll (to add  [success symbol] ) or on the Tinge roll, they
must face the effects of the Tinge (see “Tinge
Effects”).
3.	If the opponent has received  [Tinge]  by blocking
the spell, they must face the effects of the
Tinge (see “Tinge Effects”).
Blocking a Spell
During the second step of the spellcasting
process, the opposing player may declare that
they will attempt to block it with their own
Spellcaster unit – in which case, the WP roll step
will become a Face to Face Roll against 3 [black die] .
For each  [hollow block symbol]  the blocker rolls, their Spellcaster
receives 1 [Tinge] . If it receives at least 1 [Tinge] , the
Spellcaster must apply the effects of the Tinge
in the “Apply the Consequences of the Tinge”
step.
You cannot try to block a spell more than
once or with more than one unit.
62

63.text:
Tinge Roll
To perform a Tinge roll, follow these steps:
1.	Create the Tinge roll. Take as many  [black die]  dice
as indicated by the cost of the applied
alterations – but remember that the
maximum is always 3 [black die]  dice, even if the
alterations add up to more.
2.	Perform the Tinge roll. For each  [hollow block symbol]  obtained,
the Spellcaster receives 1 [Tinge] .
Tinge Effects
When a unit must face the effects of the Tinge,
consult the following table and apply the effects
from the row corresponding to the number of
[Tinge]  tokens the unit has.
TABLE OF TINGE EFFECTS
Tinge
Effects
1-4
Suffer 1 stress.
5-6
Suffer 1 stress and 1 [damage] .
The unit is destroyed. All units
7+
within 5 strides receive 1 [Tinge] .
63

64.text:
Units that belong to the Scions of Yaldabaoth
faction will use the following table instead of
the general one.

SCIONS OF YALDABAOTH

Roll 1 [orange die]  die and apply the

The unit is destroyed. All units
